passages.heading: Bundle size limits
passages.text:
Vercel places restrictions on the maximum size of the deployment bundle for functions to ensure that they execute in a timely manner.
For Vercel Functions, the maximum uncompressed size is 250 MB including layers which are automatically used depending on runtimes. These limits are enforced by AWS. For Python functions, the maximum uncompressed size is 500 MB.

passages.heading: Bundle size limits
passages.text: You can use includeFiles and excludeFiles to specify items which may affect the function size. These configurations are not supported in Next.js, instead use outputFileTracingIncludes.

passages.heading: Troubleshooting the 250 MB limit
passages.text:
When a function exceeds the limit, the build fails with this error:
txt
The Vercel Function "api/hello" is 300mb uncompressed which exceeds the maximum uncompressed size limit of 250mb.

passages.heading: Troubleshooting the 250 MB limit
passages.text:
If your project is eligible for large functions, the function can deploy without other changes once large functions are enabled. To find out what's making a function large, add the VERCEL_ANALYZE_BUILD_OUTPUT environment variable with the value 1 and redeploy. The build logs then list each function's uncompressed size and its largest files:
txt
Function : /api
Size : 1991.54 MB
Large dependencies:
• _vendor/tensorflow/libtensorflow_cc.so.2: 972.15 MB
• _vendor/tensorflow/include: 307.87 MB

passages.heading: Large functions Beta
passages.text:
Large functions let you deploy uncompressed bundles up to 5 GB. Use them for workloads that ship large dependencies, model files, or binaries. Large functions are supported on Node.js, Bun, and Python runtimes.
Large functions require fluid compute with Active CPU enabled. Fluid compute is enabled by default for new projects.

passages.heading: Supported runtimes
passages.text:
Large functions are supported on the following runtimes:
- nodejs
- bun
- python
Note: Large functions are supported for projects using
Secure Compute or
Static IPs. They are not yet supported with
BYOC.

passages.heading: Node.js, Bun, and Python runtimes
passages.text:
| | Default | Maximum | Extended maximum |
| Hobby | 300s (5 minutes) | 300s (5 minutes) | - |
| Pro | 300s (5 minutes) | 800s | 1800s (30 minutes) Beta |
| Enterprise | 300s (5 minutes) | 800s | 1800s (30 minutes) Beta |
Note: The 800 second maximum is generally available for Pro and Enterprise teams.

passages.heading: Edge runtime
passages.text: Vercel Functions using the Edge runtime must begin sending a response within 25 seconds to maintain streaming capabilities beyond this period, and can continue streaming data for up to 300 seconds.

passages.heading: Memory size limits
passages.text:
| | Default | Maximum |
| Hobby | 2 GB / 1 vCPU | 2 GB / 1 vCPU |
| Pro / Enterprise | 2 GB / 1 vCPU | 4 GB / 2 vCPU |
Users on Pro and Enterprise plans can configure the default memory size for all functions in the dashboard.
The maximum size for a Function includes your JavaScript code, imported libraries and files (such as fonts), and all files bundled in the function.

passages.heading: Request body size
passages.text: The maximum payload size for the request body or the response body of a Vercel Function is 4.5 MB. The response body limit doesn't apply to streamed responses. If a Vercel Function receives a payload in excess of the limit it will return an error 413: FUNCTION_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE. See How do I bypass the 4.5MB body size limit of Vercel Functions for more information.

passages.heading: File descriptors
passages.text: File descriptors are unique identifiers that the operating system uses to track and manage open resources like files, network connections, and I/O streams. Think of them as handles or references that your application uses to interact with these resources. Each time your code opens a file, establishes a network connection, or creates a socket, the system assigns a file descriptor to track that resource.

passages.heading: File descriptors
passages.text:
Vercel Functions have a limit of 1,024 file descriptors shared across all concurrent executions. This limit includes file descriptors used by the runtime itself, so the actual number available to your application code will be strictly less than 1,024.
File descriptors are used for:
- Open files
- Network connections (TCP sockets, HTTP requests)
- Database connections
- File system operations

passages.heading: Cost and usage
passages.text:
Active CPU time is based on the amount of CPU time your code actively consumes, measured in milliseconds. Waiting for I/O (e.g. calling AI models, database queries) does not count towards active CPU time. Provisioned memory time is based on the memory allocated to your function instances multiplied by the time they are running.
It is important to make sure you've set a reasonable maximum duration for your function. See "Managing usage and pricing for Vercel Functions" for more information.
